summary: Identifying locations on Earth with environmental and surface characteristics similar to those of potential future permanent bases and landing sites on the Moon and Mars is essential for saving time and resources in space exploration. As the SPACE STARS team, we developed a simulation interface that compares images of the lunar and Martian surfaces with visually similar locations on Earth. Using NASA's open data sources, particularly the Global Imagery Browse Services (GIBS), we developed our system with Python, FastAPI, OpenCV, and NumPy. Our interface ranks similar images of Earth's surface in response to an uploaded image from Mars and displays the similarity percentages between them. We also incorporated topographic comparisons into the process, enabling the identification of locations with similar elevation, slope, and landform characteristics. This allows research and testing planned for the Moon and Mars to be conducted in advance in comparable environments on Earth. Our project offers a technological solution aimed at reducing the time and costs associated with preparing future space missions. SPACE STARS – Project Description

Our project was developed as an image comparison and simulation interface to help identify locations on Earth with characteristics similar to potential future bases and landing sites on the Moon and Mars.

In our system, we used an image captured from the surface of Mars or the Moon as input. Using NASA's open data sources, particularly the Global Imagery Browse Services (GIBS), we developed a system that scans, compares, and ranks images of locations on Earth's surface based on their visual similarity. In this way, we developed a technological solution that enables tests required before space missions to be conducted in comparable environments on Earth.

We used Python, FastAPI, OpenCV, and NumPy technologies in developing the project. We utilized FastAPI and Uvicorn for backend operations, OpenCV and NumPy for image processing, and HTML, CSS, and JavaScript for the user interface.

The creative aspect of our project lies in developing an interactive comparison system that brings together images of extraterrestrial surfaces and potential terrestrial analog sites. Through the interface we developed, we made image similarities visible and facilitated the identification of potential terrestrial analog locations.

Our project aimed to reduce time and costs in space exploration and make testing processes more accessible by utilizing similar environments on Earth. We considered the importance of environmental similarities, surface characteristics, and available resources highlighted in NASA's challenge. In the subsequent development stages, we planned to integrate topographic features into the system and compare criteria such as elevation, slope, crater structure, and landforms. In this way, we aimed to transform our image comparison system into a more comprehensive tool for identifying terrestrial analog sites.
